title: Making Meaning of Polysubstance Use: Participant Interpretation of Data Science Outputs Within the Intersectional Risk Environment
content: Network and cluster analysis are commonly used to describe polysubstance use patterns; however, these approaches are often interpreted without grounding in lived experience. In the context of an unstable and contaminated drug supply in the United States, there is a critical need to situate quantitative findings within the social and structural conditions that shape drug use. We conducted a convergent mixed-methods study with adults reporting non-prescribed drug use in the past 12 months in a large U.S. city. Participants (N=164) completed surveys assessing substance use and polysubstance co-use. Network and cluster analyses identified patterns of co-use. A subset of participants (n=9) engaged in results-elicitation interviews in which they interpreted cluster visualizations. Qualitative analysis centered on participants’ interpretations as analytic data, informed by risk environment and intersectionality frameworks. Participants interpreted clusters as representations of collective care, racialized survival, neighborhood trust, pragmatic harm reduction, and identity navigation and self-regulation, rather than pharmacological groupings or causal pathways. Interpretations varied by intersectional position, highlighting how race, gender identity, class, and trauma shape both exposure to risk and access to protection. Polysubstance clusters reflect adaptation to intersectional risk environments rather than individual pathology.
